claim: Why not one democratic state for everyone?

heard.who: Edward Said, Palestinian scholar, in an Atlantic interview (1999)
heard.quote: One person, one vote, and let's have a truth and reconciliation commission.

heard.who: Peter Beinart, writer, in Jewish Currents (2020)
heard.quote: It is time for liberal Zionists to abandon the goal of Jewish-Palestinian separation and embrace the goal of Jewish-Palestinian equality.

answer: One state with equal votes would put Jews and Arabs at or near parity. Israel counts 7.79 million Jews and 'others' and 2.16 million Arabs; the Palestinian bureau counts 5.56 million in the West Bank and Gaza, East Jerusalem's Arabs in both. Yoram Ettinger of the American-Israel Demographic Research Group calls the Palestinian count inflated; DellaPergola and Soffer reject that. In DellaPergola's long-run 2024 projection, adding the West Bank to Israel leaves Jews about 60 percent, and adding Gaza just above 50. Israeli parties such as Yashar! say they cannot risk the Jewish majority; one-state advocates such as Said and Beinart ask for equal votes. Our reading: one state with equal votes risks a Jewish majority, annexation without votes denies equal rights, and two states on the 1967 lines would keep both at the price of a border; the numbers explain the choice, they do not make it.

facts.text: Inside Israel's own count, the Central Bureau of Statistics reported on the eve of Independence Day 2026 a population of 10.244 million: 7.790 million Jews and 'others' (76 percent), 2.157 million Arabs (21.1 percent) and about 296,000 foreigners. 'Others' are mainly immigrants under the Law of Return who are not Jews in the population register; Arabs include Muslims, Arab Christians and Druze.

facts.text: The Palestinian figures are disputed. In 2005-06 a study by the American Research Initiative, presented by the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs, said the Palestinian Authority's population was 2.4 million, not the 3.8 million the PCBS reported; Yoram Ettinger, a member of the American-Israel Demographic Research Group, said in 2015 that the PCBS overstated the West Bank by 1.1 million. Demographers Sergio DellaPergola and Arnon Soffer rejected this: DellaPergola wrote in 2007 that the American Research Initiative's case rests on 'several assumptions, including that of a hugely exaggerated Palestinian base population', and Soffer accused Ettinger of drawing conclusions to serve a right-wing agenda.

facts.text: The standard two-state version is two states on the 1967 lines with mutually agreed swaps: President Obama said so in 2011, the 2000 Clinton Parameters proposed a Palestinian state in 94 to 96 percent of the West Bank with swaps, and the September 2025 UN declaration endorsed 142 to 10 calls for a sovereign, viable Palestinian state.

facts.text: The polls: in the joint Pulse of 2024, 21 percent of Israeli Jews and 40 percent of Palestinians supported two states, a quarter of Palestinians and 14 percent of Israeli Jews supported one state with equal rights, and 42 percent of Israeli Jews supported 'annexation of the West Bank without equal rights for Palestinians'; in the Peace Index of November 2025, Jewish support for two states was 20 percent and for a binational state with equal rights 9 percent; in Gallup's 2026 survey 26 percent of Israelis and 32 percent of West Bank and East Jerusalem Palestinians supported two states; in the Palestinian Center's October 2025 poll, 47 percent of Palestinians preferred two states on the 1967 borders, 18 percent a confederation and 12 percent one state with equality.

facts.text: In numbers, what each outcome means for a Jewish majority and for equal rights, by DellaPergola's 2024 projection (which uses the CBS intermediate scenario): Israel alone, about 80 percent Jewish, can be Jewish and democratic; with the whole West Bank added the Jewish share falls to about 60 percent, which he says makes a 'Jewish and democratic state uncertain' before a binational reality; with Gaza too it falls to just above 50 percent, which 'would end the project of the Jewish state'. Smotrich's plan reaches a Jewish majority by leaving Palestinian population centres outside Israeli sovereignty.

contested.text: Whether a Jewish and democratic state can hold the whole territory without either giving the vote or denying it. DellaPergola: adding the West Bank keeps a Jewish majority but 'would render the idea of a Jewish and democratic state uncertain'. Smotrich: Israel can annex most of the land, keep a clear Jewish majority and stay Jewish and democratic because Palestinians would keep governing themselves through the Palestinian Authority. Critics such as the Joint List call that institutionalised apartheid, and Beinart argues that Israeli Jews' revealed preference is already one state in which millions lack basic rights.

could_not_verify: The Palestinian bureau's own release: pcbs.gov.ps would not load for our fetcher, so the 5.56 million figure rests on the Palestinian news agency WAFA reporting it, and UN figures only for Gaza (2.1 million) and, through a UN report, for the West Bank in 2023. We did not find the UN Population Division's own table.

A current independent audit of the Palestinian count: DellaPergola's 2024 study uses his own Palestinian projection; a peer-reviewed audit of the PCBS census was mentioned in a search summary but not read.
The American-Israel Demographic Research Group's current (2024-26) estimate: we found its 2005-06 and 2015 claims only.
Soffer's own words: read only through the Georgetown Berkley Center and the Jerusalem Post. DellaPergola's 2013 AP figures (6.9 million Jews, 6.5 million Arabs) are on an undated page.

Parties' platforms: Likud declined to answer the Ynet questionnaire and its platform was not read; Fatah's own platform and Edward Said's New York Times article were not read (we cite his Atlantic interview); Smotrich's 2017 Decisive Plan text could not be reached, so we quote his 2025 statements; Hamas's text is on the earlier card.
Whether the Palestinian Authority or Fatah supports 1967 lines with swaps in its own words: the UN page quoting Abbas does not say so; we have no read Palestinian primary document on that.

Fewer than three reliable sources: the CBS fact has two plus a government source; the Palestinian count has two plus a Palestinian government source; the double-counting fact; the confederation fact (one news, one opinion, one advocacy); the one-state and annexation facts rest on interviews and opinion pieces by the proponents themselves, which is the point of the quote but is not independent confirmation.
Pew and Gallup polls on one state: neither asks the question; only the Pulse, the Peace Index and PCPSR do.

The Israeli right's one-state proposals with citizenship for Palestinians (annexation with equal rights) are not on the card, only annexation without votes; the card has no Fatah or Palestinian Authority statement on one state versus two beyond Abbas's UN speech.
The 2014 Palestinian bureau figures (4.62 million in the West Bank and Gaza) on the INSS/Jerusalem Post page are a different year from the 2025 figures on F1 and do not support them.
not_claimed: The numbers do not decide what is just: a population's size does not settle whether its members should have equal rights, a state of their own, or a veto over the other's.

It does not claim that parity exists: the counts range from about 48 percent Jewish to about 60 percent depending on who counts, what is included (Gaza, East Jerusalem, 'others', foreign workers) and what year.
It does not say any party's position is the position of its voters, or that polls predict what any people will accept in practice.
It does not say Smotrich's plan is the Israeli government's policy, or that Said and Beinart speak for Palestinians or for Jews.
Listing who rejects which outcome does not by itself assign blame.

answer_claims.says: One state with equal votes would put Jews and Arabs at or near parity.
Israel counts 7.79 million Jews and 'others' and 2.16 million Arabs; the Palestinian bureau counts 5.56 million in the West Bank and Gaza, East Jerusalem's Arabs in both.
Yoram Ettinger of the American-Israel Demographic Research Group calls the Palestinian count inflated; DellaPergola and Soffer reject that.
In DellaPergola's long-run 2024 projection, adding the West Bank to Israel leaves Jews about 60 percent, and adding Gaza just above 50.
Israeli parties such as Yashar! say they cannot risk the Jewish majority; one-state advocates such as Said and Beinart ask for equal votes.

Our reading: one state with equal votes risks a Jewish majority, annexation without votes denies equal rights, and two states on the 1967 lines would keep both at the price of a border; the numbers explain the choice, they do not make it.

skeptic.notes: Read at least two sources per fact in context; all 54 quotes are on their pages. Who counted what: Israel's CBS counts 7.79 million 'Jews and others' (it includes non-Jewish immigrants and household members, not only Jews) and 2.157 million Arabs; the 5.56 million is the Palestinian bureau (PCBS) figure for end-2025 and the card could read it only through WAFA, a Palestinian government agency; every Palestinian figure on the card (WAFA, UN settlements report for the West Bank) traces to PCBS, and OCHA's 2.1 million is Gaza only and appears in a sentence about displacement, so F1 has one underlying source. The Israeli figure traces to CBS (F0 has CBS, Ynet quoting CBS, and DellaPergola using CBS projections). Parity check: 7.79 versus 2.16 + 5.56 minus about 0.3-0.4 million East Jerusalem Arabs counted twice (the claim rests on one hedged line by Kobi Michael, 2015, and is not confirmed by the UN page cited beside it) gives rough parity only if 'others' are counted as Jews, which the contested note about core definition says. The 'about half of the whole area' comes from a 2013-era AP page (undated) and Soffer's old projection, while the 60 percent and 'just above 50' are DellaPergola's 2024 long-run projection, so the answer mixes a present count and a projection; reworded to say 'long-run projection'. Strongest Palestinian objection: the card's annexation case is Smotrich and an unnamed backbencher; the Israeli right's annexation-with-citizenship proposals and Fatah/PA positions are absent, so 'which parties on each side back which outcome' is incomplete for the Palestinian side (Abbas's UN line and Hamas only). Strongest Israeli objection: the Palestinian count is disputed by Ettinger and the American Research Initiative (60 percent Jewish) and the card gives their case through an advocacy page and a hedged 2015 JPost quote, while the rebuttals (DellaPergola 2007, Soffer) are older; the card does not say the PCBS counts emigrants abroad as residents (Ettinger's 400,000 claim is on the JPost page). Fixed by me: Berkley Center essay is a blog repost by two named authors originally in the National Catholic Reporter, not scholarship; relabelled other, which leaves F3 and F4 with two reliable sources each. F7 has two reliable sources (My Jewish Learning is advocacy). F0 has two reliable (CBS is government). Wire: Ynet/AP and Global News/Reuters already marked. MUST-FIX: (1) Palestinian-side parties' positions from their own documents; (2) a current PCBS or UN Population Division source for 5.56 million; (3) third reliable sources for F0, F1, F3, F4, F7; (4) a second source for the East Jerusalem overlap; (5) an Israeli-right one-state-with-citizenship source.

citer.notes: Split into six sentences, each tied to facts. Removed: 'Demographers DellaPergola and Soffer put Jews at about half of the whole area' (dated 2013-era pages, no fact carries a current figure; replaced by DellaPergola's 2024 projection, which F4 and F12 carry); 'Israelis say they cannot give up a Jewish majority, Palestinians equal rights' (the Palestinian half is not carried by any fact; reworded to what F9, F12, F5 carry); 'the American-Israel Demographic Research Group says' reworded to Ettinger, a member, as F3 states; the claim that two states 'keeps both' moved inside 'Our reading' since no fact asserts it. Answer within 150 words. Holds for the answer as worded; the card stays draft because the skeptic verdict is weakened.
